### Analysis of influencing factors on teachers’ AI literacy under the SOR framework: An empirical study based on PLS‑SEM and fsQCA

**Yimin Ning1**[ ** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0002-6491-0906) **Hanyi Zheng2 · Hongde Wu3 · Zhijie Jin4 · Haibin Chang5 · Tommy Tanu Wijaya**[^6]

Received: 5 January 2025 / Accepted: 19 February 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025

## Abstract This study, grounded in the stimulus-organism-response (SOR) theory, aims to explore how stimulus factors (school support) influence cognitive organisms (psy- chological resilience, self-efficacy, attitude toward AI, and acceptance of AI), which in turn enhance behavioral responses (AI literacy), while also examining the detri- mental effects of AI anxiety. A cross-sectional design was employed, utilizing sam- ple data from 1,518 teachers. The results of PLS-SEM indicate that school support exerts a significant positive impact on psychological resilience, self-efficacy, atti- tude toward AI, and acceptance of AI. These cognitive factors, in turn, significantly enhance AI literacy. However, while AI anxiety negatively affects these cognitive factors, it does not exhibit a significant direct impact on AI literacy. Additionally, the study reveals the mediating roles of psychological resilience, self-efficacy, atti- tude toward AI, and acceptance of AI in the relationship between school support and AI literacy. The findings of fsQCA identify five high-level configurational pathways and one non-high-level pathway, demonstrating an asymmetric relationship between these configurations. The consistency values of all six pathways exceed 0.9, indicat- ing that these configurations are sufficient conditions influencing teachers’ AI lit- eracy. This study provides a theoretical framework for analyzing factors affecting teachers’ AI literacy and offers practical guidance for policy interventions and inno- vative practices to enhance teachers’ AI literacy.

**Keywords** Stimulus-organism-response · AI literacy · School support · Psychological resilience · Self-efficacy · Attitude · Acceptance

## 1 Introduction

In the field of education, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has brought transformative changes, providing innovative tools and methods to enhance teaching effective- ness and reshape learning approaches (Airaj, [2024;](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process) Chiu et al., [2024)](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process).The rapid advancement of technology has introduced new demands for teachers’ skills and competencies, particularly emphasizing the urgent need to develop AI literacy (Du et al., 2024). The OECD Future of Education and Skills 2030 initiative has explored how AI is redefining the roles and professional development of teach- ers, underscoring the importance of equipping educators with the ability to uti- lize and critically evaluate AI tools (Robertson & Beech, 2024). AI literacy for teachers not only encompasses the understanding and practical use of AI tools but also involves integrating these technologies effectively into teaching practices to improve educational quality (Kim, 2024). However, the current state of teacher training in AI literacy remains underdeveloped, with even negative perceptions surrounding teacher-AI interactions in education (Mochizuki & Vickers, 2024). A recent global survey conducted by UNESCO across more than 450 schools and universities revealed that fewer than 10% of institutions have implemented poli- cies or formal guidance regarding generative AI (Mochizuki & Vickers, 2024). In response to these challenges, researchers and policymakers have begun to advo- cate for greater attention and investment in AI literacy training for teachers. The cultivation of teachers’ AI literacy requires urgent attention, not only through the effective design and implementation of training programs but also by deeply understanding the key factors influencing teachers’ AI literacy and their underly- ing mechanisms (Zhang & Zhang, [2024)](#authors-and-affiliations). Using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) as a theoretical framework, Kim and Lee (2022) investigated in-service teachers’ acceptance and use of artificial intelligence. Their study revealed that school support and resources play a critical role in shaping teach- ers’ intentions to use AI in instructional practices. Similarly, a survey conducted by Nazaretsky et al. examined the trust and attitudes of K-12 teachers toward adopt- ing AI educational technologies (AI-EdTech). The findings indicated that enhancing teachers’ theoretical and practical knowledge of AI in educational contexts signifi- cantly increased their trust in AI-EdTech within K-12 education (Nazaretsky et al., 2022). Research has also shown that teachers’ self-efficacy in learning AI is a direct determinant of their engagement in AI learning behaviors (S. Wang et al., 2023a, 2023b, 2023c). Additionally, Hsu et al. (2023) found a significant negative correla- tion between the level of anxiety that primary and secondary school teachers experi- ence when learning AI and their self-efficacy in learning machine learning. Although existing research has explored various factors influencing teachers’ AI literacy from different perspectives, including school support, psychological traits, and AI anxiety, these factors work synergistically to enhance AI teaching capabilities. However, the specific mechanisms of this synergy remain underex- plored (Ng et al., 2023). In particular, there is a lack of research examining the interactive relationships between stimuli, organism, and response based on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) framework.

This study aims to address the identified research gap by employing the SOR framework to systematically examine the key factors influencing teachers’ AI liter- acy and their underlying mechanisms. Specifically, the study conceptualizes school support as the "Stimulus (S)" and considers teachers’ psychological traits—such as psychological resilience, self-efficacy, attitude toward AI, and acceptance of AI— as the "Organism (O)". These factors are collectively analyzed to determine how their interactions influence teachers’ AI literacy, the "Response (R)". Additionally, AI anxiety is incorporated as a stressor to evaluate its role in the overall framework. By adopting this theoretical perspective, the study not only reveals the independent effects of each factor but also explores their synergistic interactions, offering a more nuanced analysis of the pathways to improving teachers’ AI literacy. The research employs a combination of Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA). This method- ological integration addresses the limitations of traditional approaches in uncovering complex interactive relationships and provides education practitioners and policy- makers with diverse and flexible intervention strategies. Through this exploration, the study is expected to deepen theoretical understanding of the factors influencing teachers’ AI literacy and offer data-driven, scientific insights to support its develop- ment. Ultimately, it seeks to promote the effective integration and innovative appli- cation of AI technologies in the field of education.

## 2 Literature review

### 2.1 Factors influencing teachers’ AI literacy

The factors influencing teachers’ AI literacy involve three dimensions: environmen- tal, psychological, and behavioral. Environmental factors provide external support and resource guarantees for improving AI literacy. Psychological factors, as intrin- sic motivations, play an important role in promoting or inhibiting the development of AI literacy. Behavioral variables reflect the specific manifestations of teachers’ AI literacy in teaching. These factors interact in the formation and development of teachers’ AI literacy, offering important references for teacher training and policy formulation.

School support serves as a crucial external condition for enhancing teachers’ AI literacy. Research has demonstrated that investments by schools in technological equipment, training opportunities, and policy support significantly impact the devel- opment of teachers’ AI literacy (Chen et al., [2022;](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process) Luckin et al., 2022; Ottenbreit- Leftwich et al., 2018). In a qualitative study involving Chinese teachers, Kim found that teachers play a pivotal role throughout the teaching process, and robust AI tech- nology support enables them to refine various skills to adapt to classroom needs (Kim, 2024). Additionally, AI training provided by schools helps teachers enhance their AI innovation capabilities, encouraging more active application of AI tech- nologies in their teaching practices (Zhang & Zhang, [2024)](#authors-and-affiliations). A quasi-experimental study conducted by Sun et al. (2023) with K-12 computer teachers, based on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, revealed 

that targeted AI skills training significantly improves teachers’ AI literacy, teaching skills, and self-efficacy in AI-integrated instruction. Furthermore, school support not only directly enhances teachers’ AI literacy but also reduces their fear of technology use, thereby fostering their willingness to integrate AI technologies into their teach- ing (Ertmer et al., 2012; Hopcan et al., 2024).

Psychological factors are the core internal drivers influencing the development of AI literacy among teachers. These factors primarily include psychological resilience, self-efficacy, attitude toward AI, acceptance of AI, and AI anxiety (Kim & Hur, 2024; Pagán-Garbín et al., 2024; Yang & Appleget, 2024; Yim & Wegerif, 2024). Research has shown that attitude toward AI and acceptance of AI significantly influence teachers’ ability to master and apply AI technologies, with a reciprocal relationship observed (Yue et al., 2024). Psychological resilience and self-efficacy are critical abilities for teachers to face challenges posed by emerging technologies such as AI (Kowitarttawatee & Limphaibool, 2022). Psychological resilience ena- bles teachers to adapt more effectively to changes in AI-driven educational environ- ments. A case study by Musa and Nurhayati (2024) demonstrated that psychological resilience is essential for teachers to navigate the complexities of modern informa- tion technology and education systems, with teachers possessing higher psychologi- cal resilience showing greater creativity and persistence when facing technological transformation. Self-efficacy reflects teachers’ confidence in their ability to master and apply AI technologies. In a study involving 212 preschool teachers in the United States, Lim found a positive correlation between digital literacy, self-efficacy, and perceptions of AI in early childhood education. Moreover, the study highlighted that technology application, interactive learning, and problem-solving skills significantly influenced self-efficacy and its impact on perceptions of AI (Lim, 2023). Accept- ance of AI determines whether teachers will apply AI in future teaching practices (Al Darayseh, [2023)](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process); Conversely, AI anxiety, as a negative psychological factor, lim- its teachers’ willingness to innovate by fostering resistance to technology, thereby impeding the improvement of AI literacy (Hopcan et al., 2024).

AI literacy is critical behavioral variables for assessing the level of technology application among teachers. In the context of educational digital transformation and the integration of intelligent technologies into education, these two elements are of paramount importance. Broadly defined, AI literacy encompasses two essential components: AI learning skill and AI teaching skill. AI learning skill refers to teach- ers’ capacity to acquire, understand, and update their knowledge of AI technologies, including staying informed about advancements and developing skills to use AI tools effectively (Markauskaite et al., 2022; Ng et al., 2021a, 2021b). AI learning skill emphasizes teachers’ ability to apply theoretical knowledge of AI to the design of instructional frameworks and teaching materials, rather than its direct application in classroom teaching practices (Ng et al., 2024). High levels of AI literacy enable teachers to better anticipate technological trends and provide students with learning environments that align with future demands. AI teaching skill, in contrast, repre- sents the practical application of AI literacy in specific educational settings. It serves as a direct indicator of whether teachers can flexibly employ AI to meet the demands of real-world teaching scenarios (Nazaretsky et al., 2022; Seufert, Burkhard, et al., 2021). AI teaching skill encompasses various aspects of teaching practice, including 

classroom management using AI, real-time student evaluation, and the design and implementation of AI-driven personalized learning programs (Sun et  al., 2023). Teachers with high AI teaching skill are not only able to integrate technology into daily teaching practices but also capable of tailoring interventions to meet students’ individualized needs, thereby enhancing the precision and effectiveness of instruc- tion (Holstein et al., 2019; Sharples, 2013).

### 2.2 SOR theory

The SOR theory was first introduced by Mehrabian and Russell in 1974. Originat- ing from environmental psychology, this theoretical framework has been exten- sively utilized to analyze how environmental stimuli influence individual behavioral responses through psychological processes (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974). The model emphasizes how external environmental factors (S) evoke internal cognitive or emo- tional states (O), which subsequently lead to behavioral responses (R) (Zhang et al., [2021)](#authors-and-affiliations). S refers to external environmental factors that trigger psychological and emo- tional changes in individuals. In the context of education, stimuli such as learning resources, teacher support, and the campus environment are considered key factors. O represents the psychological states and emotional responses elicited within indi- viduals by external stimuli, including cognition, emotions, and perceptions. Finally, R refers to the explicit behaviors or implicit attitudes displayed by individuals as a result of the interaction between S and O, such as students’ learning satisfaction and behavioral intentions (Yang et al., 2021).

The SOR theory has been widely applied to understand complex psychological and behavioral phenomena, particularly in analyzing learning behaviors and psy- chological responses within educational research. For instance, Wut et  al. (2024) examined factors influencing students’ willingness to participate in blended learn- ing courses in higher education. In their study, teaching presence, social presence, and cognitive presence were considered S variables, while performance expectancy, social influence, effort expectancy, and facilitating conditions were categorized as O variables. Attitude towards blended learning was identified as the R variable. Zhang et al. ([2021)](#authors-and-affiliations) explored the application of the SOR theory in understanding students’ learning satisfaction, where the learning environment (e.g., social support and inter- action) served as S variables, and self-efficacy and foundational skills were treated as O variables. Similarly, Zhao et al. ([2020)](#authors-and-affiliations) applied the SOR model to study the continuous use of MOOCs, uncovering how technological environments (e.g., inter- activity, media richness, and sociality) influenced learners’ virtual experiences. Pan- dita et al. (2021) utilized the SOR model during the COVID-19 pandemic, where the pandemic itself acted as the S variable, affecting students’ psychological states (e.g., anxiety and stress), which were classified as O variables. These psychologi- cal states subsequently influenced learning behaviors such as participation in online courses. By bridging external stimuli with internal responses, the SOR theory offers theoretical support across multiple research domains. It reveals the dynamic rela- tionships within the Stimulus-Cognition/Emotion-Behavior chain, providing a struc- tured framework for understanding complex behaviors (Aydarova, [2024)](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process).

## 3 Model conceptualization and hypothesis development

This study is based on the SOR theory and analyzes the factors influencing teachers’ AI literacy from three perspectives: S, O, and R (see Fig. [1)](#3-model-conceptualization-andhypothesis-development). H1-H11 represent 11 hypotheses, each of which denotes the relationship between two variables. First, the S factor includes school support. Second, the O factors encompass teachers’ psy- chological resilience, self-efficacy, attitude toward AI, and acceptance of AI. These psychological and cognitive traits determine how teachers perceive and respond to AI technologies. Finally, the R factor consists of AI literacy, the outcome variable that not only reflects teachers’ mastery of AI technologies but also their practical application of these technologies in teaching. Additionally, this study extends the SOR model by incorporating AI anxiety as a stressor to explore how the psychologi- cal pressure teachers face when using AI technologies influences their attitudes and acceptance of AI. In summary, in this study, school support is designed as the stim- ulus that triggers cognitive responses from the organism (psychological resilience, self-efficacy, attitude toward AI, and acceptance of AI), which in turn activates AI literacy. Furthermore, by extending the SOR model, AI anxiety is identified as a stressor that negatively impacts both the organism and AI literacy.

### 3.1 Stimulus

School support plays a critical role as a S in improving teachers’ AI literacy. The positive influence of school support on psychological resilience (H1: +) has been widely recognized in psychological research. Studies suggest that teachers with high psychological resilience are more likely to perceive challenges as opportunities for growth rather than insurmountable obstacles (Li, 2023; Xue, 2022). For example, X. Wang et al. (2024b) found that school-provided support significantly enhances indi- viduals’ psychological resilience and their ability to cope with stress. This improve- ment in psychological resilience helps teachers maintain a positive attitude toward

**Fig. 1** Conceptual model based on the SOR theory educational technology transformations, thereby enabling more effective integra- tion of AI tools (Heng & Chu, 2023). Self-efficacy, as teachers’ belief in their own abilities, is also positively influenced by school support (H2: +). This conclusion is widely supported in educational research (Cai & Tang, [2021)](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process). According to self-effi- cacy theory, when teachers perceive school support, they are more likely to believe in their ability to successfully use AI technologies. This enhanced belief not only boosts their confidence but also fosters active exploration and application of AI tools (Wang & Chuang, 2024). The positive impact of school support on attitude toward AI (H3: +) has also been well-documented. Walker et al. (2012) demonstrated that professional development and resource support provided by schools significantly improve teachers’ attitudes toward new technologies. A positive attitude is a cru- cial prerequisite for teachers’ willingness to learn and adopt AI technologies (Hop- can et al., 2024). Lastly, the positive effect of school support on acceptance of AI (H4: +) has been extensively discussed in the field of educational technology inte- gration (Zhang et al., [2023)](#authors-and-affiliations). Research emphasizes that school support and encour- agement are essential for teachers to accept and integrate new technologies. When schools provide the necessary resources, teachers are more likely to view AI tech- nologies as integral to their teaching practices, thereby enhancing their AI literacy (Du & Gao, 2022).

H1. School support positively affects psychological resilience. H2. School support positively affects self-efficacy.

H3. School support positively affects attitude toward AI. H4. School support positively affects acceptance of AI.

### 3.2 Organism

O refers to an individual’s internal states or psychological reactions, including self- efficacy, psychological resilience, attitude toward AI, and acceptance of AI. The positive impact of self-efficacy on psychological resilience (H5: +) has been exten- sively studied in the field of educational psychology (Li, 2023). Research indicates that when teachers believe in their ability to effectively use AI technologies, they are more likely to exhibit higher levels of psychological resilience to address chal- lenges in the educational environment. This enhancement in self-efficacy supports teachers in maintaining positivity and adaptability when facing difficulties, thereby strengthening their psychological resilience. Similarly, the positive influence of atti- tude toward AI on acceptance of AI (H6: +) has been validated in numerous stud- ies (Wang & Pan, 2023). Teachers with more positive attitudes toward AI are more likely to accept and integrate AI tools into their teaching practices. Such a positive attitude serves as a crucial prerequisite for teachers’ willingness to explore new instructional methods and incorporate emerging technologies. This progression is vital for fostering educational innovation and enhancing teaching quality.

H5. Self-efficacy positively affects psychological resilience. H6. Attitude toward AI positively affects acceptance of AI.

The positive influence of psychological resilience on AL (H7: +) has been validated in numerous studies (X. Wang et  al., 2024a). As a critical psycho- logical resource, psychological resilience enables teachers to maintain a posi- tive attitude and adaptability in the face of AI-driven technological changes. Psychological resilience significantly enhances individual learning and devel- opment, which also applies to teachers’ persistence and growth during the process of learning AI technologies. The positive effect of self-efficacy on AI literacy (H8: +) is supported by empirical research in the field of educational technology (Mah & Groß, 2024). Studies indicate a strong correlation between an individual’s self-efficacy and their technology acceptance and usage behav- iors. In educational contexts, teachers with higher self-efficacy are more likely to actively engage in learning and applying AI technologies, thereby improv- ing their AI literacy (Du et al., 2024). The positive impact of attitude toward AI on AI literacy (H9: +) has been widely discussed in educational technol- ogy integration research (B. Wang et al., 2023a, 2023b, 2023c). Teachers with more positive attitudes toward AI are more inclined to actively learn and acquire related knowledge and skills. This finding aligns with the Technology Accept- ance Model (TAM), which posits that an individual’s attitude toward technology is a significant predictor of their usage behavior (Bailey et al., [2022)](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process). Finally, the positive influence of acceptance of AI on AI literacy (H10: +) has been demon- strated in educational practices. Teachers with higher acceptance of AI are more likely to proactively use AI tools in their teaching, thereby enhancing their AI literacy through practical application (Schiavo et al., 2024). This process aligns with the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), which emphasizes the roles of performance expectancy and effort expectancy in tech- nology acceptance (Budhathoki et al., [2024)](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process).

H7. Psychological resilience positively affects AI literacy. H8. Self-efficacy positively affects AI literacy.

H9. Attitude toward AI positively affects AI literacy. H10. Acceptance of AI positively affects AI literacy.

### 3.3 Response

The negative influence of AI anxiety on AI literacy (H11: -) has been a signifi- cant topic in the fields of educational psychology and educational technology. Research indicates that when teachers experience anxiety about AI technolo- gies, this anxiety can hinder their ability to learn and apply these tools (Hopcan et al., 2024). For instance, teachers may feel uneasy about their ability to mas- ter AI tools or worry that AI technologies might replace their roles, leading to decreased motivation and engagement in learning. This reduced motivation and participation ultimately impair their ability to develop AI literacy.

H11. AI anxiety negatively affects AI literacy.

## 4 Methodology

### 4.1 Sample and data collection

The sample was drawn from a group of teachers who participated in a one-year training program. This program was designed to develop teachers’ AI literacy and its application in teaching practices and included educators from diverse backgrounds across the country. All participants successfully completed the year-long AI-focused training. Following the training, these teachers had either begun or planned to incor- porate AI tools and technologies into their teaching practices. The sample comprised data from 1,518 teachers, as detailed in Table [1.](#4-methodology) Of the participants, 75.42% were female and 24.58% were male. Regarding teaching levels, 38.60% taught in kinder- gartens, 22.79% in primary schools, 25.89% in middle schools, and 13.90% in high schools. In terms of teaching experience, 28.85% of teachers had 0–5 years of expe- rience, 11.79% had 6–10 years, 13.44% had 11–15 years, 15.22% had 16–20 years, and 30.70% had 21–25 years. Overall, the sample demonstrated good representative- ness and diversity, providing a solid foundation for analyzing the factors influencing teachers’ AI literacy. Given the reliance on single-source, self-reported survey data, the potential for Common Method Bias (CMB) was examined following statistical guidelines (Podsakoff et al., 2024). The percentage of variance explained by the first common factor was found to be below 20%, indicating that severe CMB was not present.

### 4.2 Strategy for model indicators

To investigate teachers’ AI literacy and psychological responses, a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) was used as the data collection tool. The questionnaire consisted of two sections: one focused on self-reported basic information (i.e., gender, teaching level, and teaching age), and the other collected responses related to variables influencing AI literacy. measured using previously validated surveys or scales developed based on the con- textual background of the study. Specifically, school support was measured using the organizational support and technical support subdimensions from F. Wang et al., (2024a, 2024b, 2024c, 2024d); psychological resilience was measured using the scale revised by Kong et al. (2024); self-efficacy was measured using the self-effi- cacy scale from Yao and Wang (2024); attitude toward AI was measured using the Attitude scale from Merjovaara et al. (2024); acceptance of AI was measured using the scale from Dahri et al. (2024); AI literacy, divided into AI learning ability and AI teaching ability, was measured using the scales from Sun et al. (2023) and Ning et al. (2024), respectively. AI anxiety was measured using items developed by Schi- avo et al. (2024) and revised to align with teachers’ psychological development char- acteristics in the context of AI. To address the subjectivity of self-reports, an open- ended task was included to objectively assess teachers’ AI literacy. The task was as follows: “Please select a teaching theory suitable for an AI classroom (e.g., the ARCS model) and design a teaching framework aligned with this theory. Ensure the framework integrates AI elements into classroom teaching.” Logit regression anal- ysis revealed a correlation coefficient of 0.853 between the subjective self-assess- ments and objective test scores, indicating good consistency between subjective and objective evaluations.

In this study, the Smartpls software was used to test the reliability and validity of the measurement indicators. The model’s reliability and validity were evaluated by calculating the “Outer loadings”, “Cronbach’s alpha”, “composite reliability (CR)”, and “average variance extracted (AVE)” for the model’s constructs (Zhou et  al., [2024)](#authors-and-affiliations). As shown in Table 2, the Cronbach’s alpha and CR values for the seven con- structs were all greater than the recommended threshold of 0.7, and the AVE values exceeded 0.5. These results indicate that the scale has good reliability and validity, confirming that the measurement is reliable.

### 4.3 Data analysis

Before conducting data analysis, violin plots were used to evaluate the distribution of the data (see Fig. [2)](#512-structural-model-evaluation). The distributions of school support, psychological resilience, and self-efficacy were relatively similar, primarily concentrated in the higher range (between 3 and 4), suggesting that these variables may share similar characteristics or be influenced by common factors. The distributions of attitude toward AI, accept- ance of AI, and AI literacy were slightly more dispersed but remained centered in the moderate range, indicating moderate variability. In contrast, the distribution of AI anxiety was the narrowest, with values concentrated between 3 and 4, reflect- ing lower volatility and potentially more stable influencing factors. Overall, most variables exhibited concentrated and symmetrical distributions, indicating moderate consistency and regularity in the sample data. This low variability provides a solid foundation for subsequent analysis, as reduced variation minimizes noise interfer- ence and allows for clearer examination of the relationships between variables. #### 5.1.2 Structural model evaluation

The results of the direct effects indicate that school support significantly and posi- tively influences self-efficacy (supports H1), demonstrating that school support for AI, including resources, training, and policies, can effectively enhance teachers’ self-efficacy. This finding aligns with the role of school support in promoting tech- nology adoption as emphasized by (Kearney et al., 2018). School support positively influences self-efficacy (supporting H2). According to Bandura’s Social Cognitive

Theory, external support can enhance individuals’ self-efficacy, which is consistent with our research findings (Liu et al., 2023). School support positively influences attitude toward AI and acceptance of AI (supporting H3 and H4). Attitude toward AI positively influences acceptance of AI (supporting H6). According to the Tech- nology Acceptance Model (TAM), external support can influence individuals’ atti- tudes toward technology, and attitudes toward technology can in turn influence their acceptance of technology. This further supports hypotheses H3, H4, and H6 (Scherer et al., 2019). Self-efficacy significantly and positively influences psychological resil- ience (supporting H5). The findings indicate that self-efficacy can enhance individu- als’ psychological resilience when facing AI technology, which is consistent with the results of this study (Cassidy, [2015)](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process). Psychological resilience positively influ- ences AI literacy (supporting H7). The conclusion drawn by Wang et al. (2025) pro- vides support for H7. Self-efficacy significantly and positively influences AI literacy (supports H8), suggesting that teachers with higher self-efficacy are more inclined to actively explore and learn AI-related technologies, which supports the findings of Sun et al. (2023) that self-efficacy is a key driver of technology learning. Attitude toward AI and acceptance of AI positively influence AI Literacy (supporting H9 and H10). Existing research indicates that individuals’ attitudes and acceptance of AI can affect their learning and use of AI, which in turn impacts their AI literacy. This conclusion provides support for H8. AI anxiety does not significantly influence AI literacy (not support H11), suggesting that while teacher anxiety may have some influence, it is not a direct predictor of AI literacy. This result differs from prior find- ings, potentially due to the inclusion of several direct predictors of AI literacy in the model, which may have diluted the impact of AI anxiety (Schiavo et al., 2024). The results indicate that school support is a critical factor in enhancing teach- ers’ AI-related capabilities, directly influencing AI literacy and indirectly doing so through self-efficacy and psychological resilience. As mediating variables, self- efficacy and psychological resilience not only directly affect AI literacy but also indirectly promote its development by influencing teachers’ attitude toward AI and acceptance of AI. Attitude toward AI and acceptance of AI, as essential psycho- logical factors in teachers’ adoption of AI technologies, indirectly affect AI liter- acy through mediation effects. Due to space limitations, this study only discusses mediations related to AI literacy, all of which are supported by existing research. For I2 (school support → psychological resilience → AI literacy) and I3 (school sup- port → self-efficacy → AI literacy), school support directly enhances teachers’ psy- chological resilience or self-efficacy by providing resources, training, and encour- agement, and the improvement in psychological resilience or self-efficacy enables teachers to apply AI technologies more effectively in teaching, thereby enhancing AI literacy (Kim et al., 2024; Low et al., 2025). For I6 (school support → attitude toward AI → AI literacy) and I7 (school support → acceptance of AI → AI literacy), school support enhances attitude toward AI and acceptance of AI by offering train- ing and resources, and these positive attitudes and acceptance directly promote AI literacy, increasing the likelihood of teachers adopting AI technologies in their teaching. For I9 (self-efficacy → psychological resilience →AI literacy), improved self-efficacy boosts teachers’ confidence in facing AI-related challenges, which fur- ther enhances psychological resilience, enabling teachers to apply AI technologies more effectively in teaching, thereby improving AI literacy (Meng et al., 2025). For I10 (attitude toward AI →acceptance of AI →AI literacy), teachers’ positive atti- tudes toward AI encourage greater acceptance of AI technologies, and this increased acceptance directly enhances their ability to apply AI technologies in teaching, thereby improving AI literacy (Zhang et al., [2025)](#authors-and-affiliations). For I4 (school support → self- efficacy → psychological resilience →AI literacy), school support first enhances teachers’ self-efficacy, which then strengthens psychological resilience, and together, these factors promote teachers’ AI literacy. For I8 (school support → attitude toward AI → acceptance of AI → AI literacy), school support shapes teachers’ positive atti- tudes toward AI by providing opportunities for AI application, and this positive attitude further enhances acceptance of AI. As acceptance of AI increases, teachers are more inclined to integrate AI technologies into teaching, thus improving their AI literacy (Seufert, Guggemos, et al., 2021a, 2021b). This complex indirect path- way validates the multi-level influence mechanism of the SOR model, demonstrat- ing how S impacts the final R through cognitive and behavioral mediators. These mediation effects highlight the importance of school support in fostering teachers’ self-efficacy and psychological resilience and the critical roles these factors play in promoting teachers’ adoption and application of AI technologies. The data support- ing the above conclusion can be found in Table 4.

### 5.2 Asymmetric analysis

The asymmetric analysis was conducted using fsQCA. Data calibration, a critical step in calculating the membership degree of causal variable sets, was performed using the conventional thresholds of 95%, 50%, and 5%. The necessity condition test, a key procedure in assessing the relationship between subset conditions and outcome conditions, determines whether a constant condition intersection exists within the result set, qualifying it as a necessary condition. This test calculates con- sistency and coverage using established algorithms, with thresholds of 0.9 and 0.5, respectively. The calibrated data analysis results, presented in Table 5, reveal that the consistency for high and low levels of AI literacy ranges from 0.500 to 0.857,

This indicates that no single variable meets the cri- teria for a necessary condition, necessitating a deeper exploration of multi-condition configurational combinations. Configurations represent combinations of conditions that lead to specific outcomes or phenomena.

This study adopted existing research findings and case-specific considerations to set the consistency threshold at 0.8, the case frequency threshold at 1, and the Proportional Reduction in Inconsistency (PRI) consistency threshold at 0.7 for con- structing the truth table (Foroughi et al., 2024). Furthermore, since prior research has not reached a consensus on the relationship between the eight conditions and high/low configuration efficiency, and there are no definitive conclusions in this study about how school support, psychological resilience, self-efficacy, and attitude toward AI influence high/low levels of AI literacy, these conditions were set to "pre- sent or absent." Using fsQCA 4.0, the configurational paths leading to high TFP in teacher groups were calculated, and the results are summarized in Table 6. Since PLS-SEM serves as a linear model to evaluate the relationships between variables, it provides conditional support for fsQCA. The results of fsQCA further validate the findings of PLS-SEM, revealing multiple configurational paths that explain the development of high-level. In the configurational paths, “●” represents core conditions, “**•**” represents peripheral conditions, “⨂” indicates the absence of core conditions, and blank spaces indicate that the presence or absence of the con- dition is inconsequential. **5.2.1 Configurational analysis of high‑level AI literacy**

Configuration 1 and configuration 2: in cases of positive attitude toward AI, the presence or absence of school support is contrasted. Teachers with high AI readi- ness often mitigate the stress caused by AI anxiety and exhibit greater AI-enhanced innovation and job satisfaction (X. H. Wang et al., 2023a, 2023b, 2023c). The data indicate that holding a positive attitude toward AI and experiencing no additional stress (i.e., low AI anxiety) explains the feasibility of achieving high-level AI lit- eracy through Configurations 1 and 2. In Configuration 1, psychological resilience is identified as a core condition, supporting the findings of Polat et  al. (2023), which highlighted the moderating role of psychological resilience in the relation- ship between organizational exclusion and burnout. Configuration 2 considers cases where schools provide no AI-related support, but teachers display positive attitude toward AI and acceptance of AI. Compared to Configuration 2, Configuration 1 shows relatively higher raw coverage, indicating stronger explanatory power and greater empirical significance in fostering high-level AI literacy.

Configuration 3: the synergistic influence of school support and teachers’ AI acceptance. Configuration 3 highlights the collaborative impact of school support and teachers’ acceptance of AI. School-provided support, such as funding, technical infrastructure, and policies aimed at fostering teachers’ AI literacy, inherently pro- motes teachers’ acceptance of AI technologies (Shen & Cui, 2024). The test results indicate that school support and acceptance of AI serve as core conditions, with atti- tude toward AI as a peripheral condition. Even in the absence of self-efficacy as a core condition, the consistency of 0.946 satisfies the threshold for a valid path to high-level AI literacy. This finding demonstrates that when external and internal conditions are both met and mutually reinforcing, the absence of self-efficacy does not significantly hinder the development of AI literacy.

Configurations 4 and configurations 5: multi-core condition composite driving high-level AI literacy. Configurations 4 and Configurations 5 demonstrate how the coupling of multiple core conditions facilitates the formation of high-level AI lit- eracy among teachers. In Configuration 5, when self-efficacy, attitude toward AI, acceptance of AI, and school support simultaneously serve as core conditions, a 

clear trend of high-level AI literacy development is observed (Pan & Wang, 2025). In Configuration 4, self-efficacy and school support act as peripheral conditions, while psychological resilience is considered the core condition. In this scenario, the absence of a positive attitude toward AI does not hinder the pathway to high-level AI literacy, as evidenced by a raw coverage of 0.550 with minimal variation. This indicates that Configuration 4 remains an effective path for achieving high-level AI literacy. The external environmental stimulus, specifically school support for AI, also drives teachers’ acceptance of AI and their willingness to use AI, thereby facili- tating the integration and management of AI in classroom practices. These findings underscore the synergistic collaboration between environmental factors and individ- ual psychological responses, which exerts a positive and direct impact on teachers’ high-level AI literacy development. Compared to the earlier configurations, these two configurations account for a more comprehensive set of core conditions, leading to more pronounced effects on teachers’ AI literacy.

**5.2.2 Configurational analysis of low‑level AI literacy**

Configuration 6: absence of core conditions.The results indicate that, in the absence of both external support and internal psychological resources, low-level AI literacy is generated regardless of whether teachers are subjected to external pressure from AI anxiety. When schools fail to provide AI resources, such as lacking the necessary equipment, not investing in or offering training courses, or lacking policies that sup- port the development of AI literacy, teachers develop resistance to AI usage (Liu & Fan, 2025). At the same time, psychological factors within the teachers act as core conditions. When teachers possess low psychological resilience, low self-efficacy, and a negative attitude toward AI with poor acceptance, the absence of these inter- nal driving forces also contributes to low-level AI literacy. Therefore, it can be con- cluded that low-level AI literacy is not caused by a single factor but rather results from the combined effects of environmental and organism-related factors. The analysis based on existing studies and the results of the fsQCA technique indicate that teachers’ AI literacy is not driven by a single factor but rather by the integration of multiple elements, highlighting the complexity of technology adop- tion (Chen et al., [2024)](#acknowledgements-thank-you-to-zhijie-jin-and-haibin-chang-for-the-guidance-in-topic-selection-and-thesis-writing-thanks-to-hanyi-zheng-for-their-substantial-assistance-in-the-data-collection-process-thanks-to-hongde-wu-for-the-substantial-help-in-the-translation-and-proofreading-process-thank-you-to-tommy-tanu-wijaya-for-the-assistance-in-the-thesis-writing-process). As demonstrated by the results, the development of high- level AI literacy among teachers can be explained by five configurations, while low-level AI literacy is associated with one configuration. In this study, the five con- figurations for high-level AI literacy are categorized into three types for analysis. The first type involves the synergy between teachers’ attitude toward AI and reduced AI anxiety. Teachers’ positive attitudes toward AI can stimulate their intrinsic moti- vation to learn and use AI. Positive psychology emphasizes the importance of posi- tive emotions and attitudes for personal development. Individual attitudes perme- ate all areas of behavior, producing long-term effects. Related studies suggest that changes in attitudes lead to changes in behavior (Verplanken & Orbell, 2022). On this basis, reducing AI anxiety further promotes the overall development of high- level AI literacy. Existing research has revealed the mediating role of persistence and resilience in the relationship between basic psychological needs and the intention to adopt AI tools for language learning (Zhai et al., [2024)](#authors-and-affiliations). This aligns with the findings of this study, which suggest that teachers with stronger psychological resilience and higher levels of perseverance are more receptive to AI, better equipped to handle stress, and more motivated to use AI, resulting in the development of high-level AI literacy through the coordination of multiple positive factors. The second type provides evidence that teachers’ acceptance of AI, in synergy with school support, drives the development of AI literacy. For example, well-equipped schools that offer appropriate training and policy support, combined with high teacher acceptance of AI in the classroom, allow AI literacy to improve continuously through classroom practices and collaborative discussions among teachers. Previous research exploring teachers’ acceptance of AI under the UTAUT2 model has shown that AI literacy and perceived ease of use are critical factors influencing teachers’ acceptance of AI for classroom use. Finally, the third type stands in stark contrast to the development of low-level AI literacy, providing reciprocal evidence of the role of multi-condition composite drivers or their absence in promoting or inhibiting teachers’ AI literacy. Teachers’ psychological conditions act as mediators between stimuli and responses, playing a critical role and further supporting the applicability of the SOR theoretical model in the context of this study.

## 6 Discussion

### 6.1 Theoretical implications

This study, grounded in the SOR theory, provides a comprehensive analysis of the formation mechanisms of teachers’ AI literacy from four dimensions: environmental factors, psychological factors, behavioral factors, and stressors (Duong et al., 2024). It offers a novel integrated perspective to the existing research. The SOR theory serves as a theoretical foundation for constructing a systematic model of teach- ers’ AI literacy, while the introduction of PLS-SEM and fsQCA methods further enriches the analytical dimensions of influencing factors. By exploring the com- plex structures and pathways influencing teachers’ AI literacy through PLS-SEM and fsQCA, this study provides practical guidance for educational administrators in developing effective teacher training and support strategies.

### 6.2 Practical implications

The findings of this study provide clear guidance for educational practice, empha- sizing the critical role of schools in enhancing teachers’ AI literacy. Schools should strengthen AI support by providing comprehensive AI technology resources, hardware, software, and professional training. This not only enhances teachers’ self-efficacy but also indirectly improves their attitude toward AI and acceptance of AI (Kim et  al., 2022; Nazaretsky et  al., 2022). Simultaneously, schools should focus on building teachers’ psychological resilience through psy- chological counseling and team collaboration, helping teachers maintain a posi- tive mindset when facing AI technology challenges. This facilitates teachers’ acceptance and application of AI technologies, leveraging self-efficacy as a medi- ating factor.Additionally, schools should encourage teachers to actively partici- pate in AI-related learning activities, such as seminars, workshops, and online courses, to foster positive AI perceptions and attitudes (Yau et al., 2023). School leaders should establish a multi-level support system that organically combines AI support, psychological resilience development, and learning opportuni- ties, creating a virtuous cycle to fully leverage the multidimensional impacts of stimuli through cognitive and behavioral mediators on the final response factors (Ghamrawi et al., 2024). Although the direct effect of AI anxiety on AI literacy is not significant, schools should still prioritize teachers’ mental health and pro- vide necessary support to ensure their growth and development in a supportive environment. Through these comprehensive measures, schools can help teachers overcome fear and uncertainty surrounding AI technologies, enhance their self- efficacy and psychological resilience, and more effectively integrate AI technolo- gies into teaching. This will ultimately improve teaching quality and efficiency, driving innovation and development in educational practices.

## 7 Limitations and future research

Although this study has made notable progress in exploring teachers’ AI literacy based on the SOR theory, further investigation is needed to deepen the understand- ing of the concept and its components. Future research could explore additional theoretical frameworks, such as Self-Determination Theory (Chiu et al., 2022), The- ory of Planned Behavior (C. Wang et al., 2024a, 2024b, 2024c, 2024d) and Social Cognitive Theory (Shu et al., 2011), to construct a more comprehensive model of teachers’ AI literacy. Additionally, while the use of PLS-SEM and fsQCA methods enriches the analysis, there may be unexamined variables or alternative methods that could further refine the understanding of teachers’ AI literacy. Future studies could also employ Hierarchical Linear Modeling (HLM) (Peng et  al., 2023) to explore the influence of multilevel variables (individual and organizational) on teachers’ AI literacy, providing insights into how both individual-level factors and institutional- level factors contribute to the development of AI literacy among teachers. This study employed a cross-sectional design; future studies could adopt longitudinal designs to track the developmental trajectory of teachers’ AI literacy and examine how fac- tors such as school support and psychological resilience influence this process over time (Kong et al., 2023). Additionally, methods such as field surveys, case studies, and follow-up experiments could be utilized to explore the practical outcomes of fostering teachers’ AI literacy, providing more reliable guidance for educational practices. Future research could also focus on individual differences among teach- ers with diverse backgrounds, such as variations in AI literacy needs and challenges based on gender, teaching level, or years of experience. Furthermore, investigations could delve into the influence of educational policies, school culture, and teacher training programs on the development of AI literacy, examining how policy inter- ventions and practical innovations can effectively enhance teachers’ AI literacy.
